questions.title: File I/O practice 1
questions.prompt: Which stream type reads from a file?
choices: std::ifstream
std::ofstream
std::cout
std::string
questions.explanation: An ifstream is an input file stream, while an ofstream sends output into a file.

questions.title: File I/O practice 2
choices: The body runs only after a successful read
It reads the entire file at once
It sorts the lines
It keeps the stream open forever
questions.explanation: The returned stream state becomes false when reading fails, preventing the loop from processing invalid data.

questions.title: Trace File I/O
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
accepted: One output line for each line in courses.txt.
questions.explanation: The loop processes each line only after getline succeeds, so it does not repeat stale data after the final read. The resulting output is 'One output line for each line in courses.txt.'.

questions.title: File I/O practice 5
questions.prompt: Why is `while (std::getline(input, line))` preferred over looping on `!input.eof()`?
choices: `getline` becomes false as soon as a read fails, so the last line is not reused.
getline reads the whole file at once, which is faster
eof() is not a real function on input streams
getline automatically skips blank lines
questions.explanation: `eof()` only becomes true *after* a read past the end has already failed, so an `eof()`-controlled loop runs one extra time with stale data. Testing `getline` directly stops the moment a read fails. It reads one line per call (not the whole file) and does not skip blank lines.

questions.title: Relative path location
questions.prompt: A C++ program opens `courses.txt` and cannot find it. What path detail should the student check?
choices: Relative paths are resolved from the program's current working directory.
Relative paths are always resolved from the folder that contains the .cpp file.
The compiler moves input files beside the executable automatically.
ifstream searches every project folder until it finds a matching file.
questions.explanation: A relative path is not automatically based on the source file's folder. It is resolved from the process working directory, which can differ between an IDE, terminal, test runner, and deployed program.

questions.title: Open succeeded
questions.prompt: What should code check before reading from an input file stream?
choices: Assume a missing file behaves like an empty file.
Check that opening succeeded.
Read one line first and only then check whether the stream opened.
Check only the filename extension, not the stream state.
questions.explanation: Opening a stream can fail because the path is wrong, permissions block access, or the file is missing. Checking the stream before reading prevents the program from processing data that was never loaded.

questions.title: Successful reads
questions.prompt: When should parsed file data be trusted?
choices: Before checking whether the file opened successfully.
After reaching end-of-file, even if the last read failed.
Process data only after a successful read.
Treat a missing file as an empty valid file every time.
questions.explanation: Trust data only after the read or parse operation reports success. File code can reach end-of-file, encounter malformed input, or fail mid-read, so later calculations need to know the data is valid.

questions.title: Working directory
questions.prompt: Why should students know the working directory for relative file paths?
choices: Write output before validating the destination.
Ignore partial read or parse failures.
Use platform-specific separators in portable code.
Know the working directory for relative paths.
questions.explanation: The working directory determines where relative paths are looked up. If the student assumes the source-code folder but the program runs elsewhere, the file may appear to be missing even when it exists.

questions.title: RAII stream cleanup
questions.prompt: How do C++ stream objects usually close files?
choices: Let stream objects close files through their destructors.
Hide the original file error behind a vague message.
Read all lines when streaming would keep memory smaller.
Assume the default charset is always the intended one.
questions.explanation: File stream objects close their files when they are destroyed. This RAII behavior means ordinary local streams clean themselves up at the end of scope, even when early returns or exceptions happen.

questions.title: Stream checks
questions.prompt: What makes C++ file reading and writing trustworthy?
choices: Mix persistence code with unrelated calculations.
Read and write files through streams with clear failure checks.
Open the same file twice for conflicting operations.
Forget that write modes can replace existing data.
questions.explanation: Use streams with clear checks around opening, reading, parsing, and writing. That keeps the code from treating missing files, failed reads, or replaced output as if everything succeeded.
